summary: A landlocked country in southwestern Central Asia, 80 percent of which is the Karakum Desert, with some of the world's largest natural gas reserves; it has followed a policy of permanent neutrality since becoming independent from the Soviet Union in 1991.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: In the mid-7th century Arab armies took the Silk Road center of Merv, and Islam arrived from then on; in the 10th century the Oghuz Turkic tribes, the ancestors of the Turkmen, converted to Islam, and the Seljuk Empire they founded in the 11th century made Merv an important capital, making Sunnism the local mainstream. The Islam of the nomadic tribes blended customs such as ancestor veneration and pilgrimage to saints' tombs. In the Soviet period mosques were closed in large numbers, and after independence in 1991 the government built large mosques, but religious activity is strictly controlled by the state.

ranking.name: Russian Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In 1881 the Russian Empire defeated the Turkmen at the Battle of Geok Tepe and conquered the area, then built the Trans-Caspian Railway, and large numbers of Russian settlers and officials came to cities such as Ashgabat, bringing Russian Orthodoxy. The Russian population kept growing in the Soviet period, but after independence in 1991 many moved to Russia, so the share of Orthodox believers fell, and they are concentrated mainly in the capital and the cities of the Caspian coast.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: Other faiths include Protestant groups and the Baháʼí Faith. Ashgabat completed the world's first Baháʼí House of Worship in 1908, which was later confiscated in the Soviet period and demolished in the 1960s. Today Turkmenistan strictly controls unregistered religious groups, so these faiths have very few followers.

religion.background: The ancient Turkmen region was home to Zoroastrianism, Buddhism and Nestorian Christianity, and Merv was a religious and commercial center on the Silk Road. Islam arrived after the Arab conquest of the 7th century, and in the 10th–11th centuries the Oghuz Turks converted and founded the Seljuk Empire, after which Sunnism became the mainstream. The Russian Empire's conquest at the end of the 19th century brought Orthodox Christianity, and the Soviet period pursued atheism and suppressed religion. After independence Islam has been regarded as part of the national tradition, but the state maintains tight control over religious organizations and education.

ranking.name: Turkmen
ranking.description: Turkmen belongs to the Oghuz branch of the Turkic family and is close to Azerbaijani and Turkish. The 18th-century poet Magtymguly wrote in Turkmen and is revered as the national poet. In the Soviet period the script was changed from the Arabic alphabet to the Latin alphabet (in 1928) and then to Cyrillic (in 1940), and after independence in 1993 it was changed back to the Latin alphabet; Turkmen make up more than 80 percent of the country, so it is the mother tongue of the majority.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russian was the main language of administration, education and urban life in the Tsarist and Soviet periods, and many Turkmen elites also received a Russian-language education. After independence in 1991 the government pursued a policy of giving priority to Turkmen, the number of Russian-language schools fell sharply, and with the emigration of large numbers of Russians, the population mainly using Russian has continued to fall, though it is still used in the capital and among the older generation.

ranking.name: Uzbek
ranking.description: Uzbeks live mainly along the Amu Darya in the northern Daşoguz Region and the eastern Lebap Region, areas that historically belonged to the Khanate of Khiva and the Khanate of Bukhara. When the Soviet Union divided the Central Asian national republics in 1924, these Uzbek-populated areas were assigned to Turkmenistan, forming today's minority community.

language.history: Turkmen derives from the language of the Oghuz Turks and was written in the Arabic alphabet in the Middle Ages, deeply influenced by Persian. The works of the 18th-century poet Magtymguly laid the foundation of Turkmen literature. In 1924 the Soviet Union established the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic, the Turkmen script was changed first to the Latin and then to the Cyrillic alphabet, and Russian became the language of administration and higher education. After independence in 1993 the country adopted a new Latin alphabet, the government strongly promoted Turkmen, and the status of Russian fell accordingly.

ranking.name: Turkmen plov
ranking.description: Lamb, onion and carrot are fried in mutton fat in a large iron cauldron, then rice is added and slowly steamed, giving glossy grains with a meaty aroma and the sweetness of carrot.
ranking.history: Plov is a dish common to the Silk Road in Central Asia, and the Turkmen region has since ancient times been a crossroads of the trade route linking Persia and Central Asia, with rice and spices arriving with the caravans. The Turkmen cook large pots of plov to entertain relatives and friends at weddings, births, religious holidays and memorial rites, symbolizing generosity and hospitality. Traditionally men set up a large cauldron outdoors to cook it, and one pot can feed a hundred people.

ranking.name: Dograma
ranking.description: Bread is torn into small pieces and put in a large bowl, hot lamb broth is poured over it, and chopped lamb, onion and tomato are mixed in, tender and soft with a fragrant broth.
ranking.history: "Dograma" means "torn up" in Turkmen, referring to the way the bread and meat are chopped. It is one of the most ceremonial dishes of Turkmenistan, often made in large quantities at the Feast of the Sacrifice, memorials for the dead and important holidays, with relatives and friends tearing the bread together, symbolizing unity and sharing. In the nomadic society of the past, with limited supplies, this way of combining bread and meat broth let everyone eat their fill.

ranking.name: Manty (dumplings)
ranking.description: Thin dough is filled with chopped lamb or beef, mutton fat and onion and steamed in a multi-tiered steamer, often served with sour yogurt or vinegar.
ranking.history: The name and method of manty are generally thought to be related to Chinese doughy foods such as "mantou," which spread to Central Asia with the exchanges of the Silk Road and Mongol Empire era and later became common among the Turkic peoples. Central Asians changed the filling to lamb and mutton fat, giving a rich, juicy flavor. In the Soviet period multi-tiered aluminum steamers became common, and manty became an even more common dish at family gatherings and holidays.

ranking.name: Gutap (stuffed flatbread)
ranking.description: Extremely thin dough is filled with minced meat, pumpkin or spinach and the like, folded into a half-moon and cooked on a dry pan, with butter spread on before it comes off.
ranking.history: Gutap is a traditional dough dish of Turkmen nomadic and farming-herding families, and the filling changes with the seasons: wild greens and spinach in spring, pumpkin in autumn, and lamb or camel meat in ordinary times. This method of quick cooking on a dry pan suits a nomadic life without large ovens. Today it is a common snack when Turkmen families entertain guests and at festivals, and different filling flavors have developed in different places.

ranking.name: Shashlik (grilled skewers)
ranking.description: Marinated pieces of lamb or beef are threaded onto iron skewers and grilled over charcoal until charred outside and tender inside, sprinkled with onion rings and spices, and eaten with flatbread.
ranking.history: The tradition of charcoal-grilled skewers among the nomadic peoples of Central Asia goes back a long way, and the name "shashlik" spread through Russian and became the common term throughout the region in the Soviet period. In Turkmenistan skewers are the most popular food at markets, roadside stalls and weekend outings, often served with green tea and flatbread. Because Turkmenistan is famous for animal husbandry, lamb skewers in particular are regarded as a fine delicacy for guests.
